respStmt.resp: traduction anglaise assistee par IA (non relue par un expert), a partir du texte grec zoo80/4g

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise produite par intelligence artificielle (Claude, Anthropic), non relue par un expert, a partir du texte grec edite dans le corpus Zoomathia (zoo80/4g.xml), lui-meme issu de l'edition des Hippiatrica (Additamenta Londinensia ad Hippiatrica Cantabrigiensia). Le texte source est un recueil composite de recettes veterinaires greco-romaines tardives (Tiberius, Pelagonius, Apsyrtos, Hierocles, Eumelos, Africanus, extraits attribues a Dioscoride, Apollonius), transmis de maniere fragmentaire; les lacunes et passages corrompus du grec sont signales entre crochets. La numerotation des chapitres suit l'ordre de lecture du texte source et non la numerotation interne, elle-meme incoherente dans l'edition.

div.head: Additamenta Londinensia to the Cambridge Hippiatrica
div.p: Additamenta Londinensia to the Hippiatrica Cantabrigiensia.
Hippiatrica.

div.head: Tiberius, on fever
div.p: Tiberius, on the same affliction, that of fever. These are the signs that fever is present: the body becomes drenched in sweat and the tips of the feet grow cold; the ears and the heart falter, the nostrils are drawn tight, and the flanks hang loose. If the third day passes and these signs persist, do not attach hope to such a case, for it will die at once. But if only the feet are cold, attach hope and expect to cure it.

The treatment to use is this: take soaked fenugreek and raisins and give them to eat, and after eating wrap the animal in blankets and walk it for one hour, then give it green fodder to eat, so as to cool it down and soothe it — for its insides are burning. Do this until it recovers.

div.head: Letter of Teuthras, ruler of the Arabs, to Tiberius Caesar, on the anatomy of the vulture
div.p: Teuthras, ruler of the Arabs, to Tiberius Caesar of the Romans, on the anatomy of the vulture [and on the four origins of fevers]. I received the costly gifts, sent through the centurion Montanius Fronto, which you thought worthy to send me, being a king. And I too have sent you, in turn, things that seemed to me to carry a value more precious to our art — things which my forefathers used for the safety and benefit of mankind, and which to this day have never been disclosed to your people. Vain indeed are the Greeks, who hunt down the vulture and treat it as an enemy, not knowing the benefits that come from it.

div.head: On the remedies drawn from the vulture (1): head, brain, liver, blood
div.p: For, in the first place, there is a remedy from the bone of its head: it cures headache when tied on the sufferer. Its brain cures what physicians call kephalaia [chronic headache], applied as an ointment with old oil and a little cedar resin, touched to the nostrils. By what means it works I could not say, but that it cures is attested by the relief itself.

Its liver, ground together with its own blood and given with oxymel for three days, or even seven, cures whoever drinks it of spitting blood. Its blood has yet another power: ground together with the root of black chameleon and applied, it cures leprosy, once cabbage leaves or beet leaves have been laid on top and made to stick.

div.head: On the remedies drawn from the vulture (2): bile, mouth, stomach, lung
div.p: Its bile, with the juice of horehound and a little Attic honey, removes every dimming and mistiness of the eyes, and does not allow incipient cataracts to form. Its mouth and stomach, dried and mixed with laurel oil, cure those harmed by cold.

Its lung, burnt over vine-wood coals with pomegranate rind, or with misy and saffron likewise, cures those who cough up blood, taken by night and at dawn. If, however, there is a low fever as well, it is given with dark wine.

div.head: On the remedies drawn from the vulture (3): tongue, beak, eye, heart
div.p: Then, tied as an amulet on children, it protects them from every apparition and evil spirit. Its tongue, tied around the neck, cures those suffering from a swollen uvula. Its beak, tied around the neck, cures those with throat ailments and dysentery.

Its eye does not allow ophthalmia to develop. Against cataracts and severe dimming and dullness of sight, tie the eyes around the neck; let them be bound in a clean linen cloth. And even if the animal suffers some other affliction while wearing this, it will feel no pain about the eyes.

div.head: On the remedies drawn from the vulture (4): heart, entrails, dung
div.p: And the heart of the creature itself, dried and burnt, becomes a relish with cumin and pepper, or with malabathrum leaf and spikenard and very sharp vinegar and garum. When you have dined and are about to sleep, if you dip a morsel of bread in this relish, mixing in enough from its belly, and then eat it, you will not suffer indigestion.
And the animal's dung, fumigated under a woman in labour, does not let the infant be held back for long.

div.head: Eye-medicine for horses and other animals, against leukoma
div.p: And you shall prepare an eye-medicine for horses and other animals: vulture bile and hare rennet and the juice of fennel and saffron, mixed together; use it against every leukoma [white spot on the eye].
You shall also prepare it another way: bile of the same creature, hare rennet, milk of a female dog, the juice of horehound, and Attic honey — grind together and use.

div.head: The four origins of fevers
div.p: There are four origins of fevers: one from fire, another from air, another from moisture, another from cold. And the one from fire is continuous, the one from air is not continuous, the one from moisture [text broken off], and the one from cold occurs every fourth day. [This was rejected as unsound.]

div.head: Tiberius, remedy for horses suffering from glanders
div.p: Tiberius, a remedy for horses suffering from glanders. If a horse is troubled by glanders, filter the root of the wild cucumber and instill it into the nostrils, and you will cure it; or tie on a piece of fine linen as an amulet.

div.head: Tiberius, another remedy for glanders
div.p: By the same author. Take the juice of the root of the wild cucumber, one egg's measure; garum made from fish, two eggs' measure; good oil, two eggs' measure; instill through the nostrils while the air is warm. First anoint the loins and the forehead.

div.head: An eye-medicine
div.p: An eye-medicine. [Lacuna in the text] ... anoint the place with the blood from the feather. Or take dates, or rose leaves, and two boiled eggs; grind the stoned dates together with the rest, and apply as a plaster; let only a little hang free.

div.head: On hypochysis (cataract)
div.p: By the same author, on hypochysis. If a horse or any other draught animal develops hypochysis in the eye, the condition is a grave one; its signs are these: on the first day the eye appears clear, but the animal sees nothing. Treat it as described above for glaucomas.

But if, while being anointed, the eye becomes bloodshot and weeps, it will recover. If, however, there shines within it, in the middle, something like the colour of Attic honey, such cases cannot be cured, because the humour has already congealed in one place. Glaucomas and hypochyses befall them from the brain and from a perforation reaching to the eye, whenever the discharge that flows down is sharp and bilious.

div.head: Pelagonius, for a gland-swelling near the eye
div.p: Pelagonius, for simblíasis [a chalazion-like swelling near the eye]. Myrrh, half an ounce; male frankincense, two ounces; Sicilian saffron, two ounces: grind and sift, then add Falernian wine and rainwater and enough Attic honey, and store it in a glass vessel; use from there.

div.head: Treatment for discharges of the eye
div.p: Treatment for discharges of the eye. Take blood from the right side of the eye and anoint with first-quality honey until complete recovery.

div.head: For a chronic leukoma
div.p: For a chronic leukoma. Roast the thin membrane from the belly of a black bird in the sun or in smoke, mix with pepper, Gangran salt, and cuttlebone, grind to powder, and blow it in through a reed; or use ground seed of the golden-cabbage plant.

div.head: For a rough leukoma
div.p: For a rough leukoma. Crush the small creature called the millipede and sprinkle it into the eye.

div.head: Treatment for when the eye closes shut
div.p: Treatment for when the eye closes shut. Grind dry human dung and sprinkle it in.

div.head: Drawing out fistulas from a deep hollow
div.p: Drawing out fistulas from a deep hollow. Roasted chalcitis, two ounces, etc.; store in a glass vessel; or mix ground frankincense with first-quality honey and use; or mix verdigris and chalcitis with honey and use.

div.head: A collyrium producing scars of even colour
div.p: The collyrium made with black vitriol that leaves scars of even colour. Grind together split alum, Egyptian acanthus, and black vitriol, and anoint after fomenting beforehand; or take the flesh of black myrtle berries, one ounce, acacia and gum, one ounce each, soak, and sprinkle on.

div.head: For glaucosis, hypochysis, and all despaired-of conditions
div.p: For glaucosis and hypochysis and all conditions given up as hopeless. Opopanax, one and a half sixths of an ounce; Indian lycium, three sixths and eighteen carats; hematite stone, one and a half sixths; Attic honey, six ounces; verbena juice, one and a half sixths; opobalsam, two sixths and six carats; goat's bile, four and a half sixths: grind the dry ingredients together with the liquid ones and use.

div.head: Another remedy for leukomata
div.p: Another for leukomata. Burnt paper with honey and pepper; or a child's dung with honey, applied; or grind the juice of tender ivy leaves and anoint with a feather; or rinse into the fasting mouth, then rinse at once with wine, so as not to harm the teeth.

Or take a mountain tortoise, put it into a new pot, burn it, make it into a powder, and blow it into the eye through a reed; or catch a grey mullet in the month of May, cut it open, and put its bile into the eye.

div.head: For excessive proud flesh growing over the eye
div.p: For excessive proud flesh growing over the eye. Burnt copper and myrrh, one ounce each; honey, six ounces: grind fine and anoint.

div.head: Very effective for hypochyses
div.p: Very effective for hypochyses. Unite in equal parts goat's bile, saffron, and Attic honey, and use.

div.head: [Text lost]
div.p: [The text at this point is reduced to an unreadable trace in the source manuscript.]

div.head: A liquid eye-medicine
div.p: A liquid eye-medicine. Mix equal parts of the juice of the sharpest onion — Cyprian onion above all — and Attic honey, put into a glass vessel, hang it in smoke, and use.

div.head: Another, made from biles
div.p: Another, made from biles. Hawk's bile, half an ounce; bile of parrotfish, partridge, cock, vulture, hyena, oriole, and frog, and the juice of fennel, half an ounce of each; Attic honey, six ounces; opobalsam, one ounce: unite all and use; or anoint with the bile of a suckling kid mixed with honey.

div.head: For hypochyses
div.p: For hypochyses. Burn barley bread thoroughly, grind with honey, and use.

div.head: For aigilops (tear-duct fistula)
div.p: For aigilops. These are cured as follows: apply the plant tzypa; or pound horehound and dock together with old pork lard and apply; or apply ground leaves of chamomile. Even the juice of this herb alone, kneaded with wheat flour, does no small good; or ground leaves of plantain.
Even theriac ground with honey and balsam helps, as do the salts used in theriac. And the tail of the stingray, anointed with honey, cures leukomata.

div.head: From Dioscorides, for a discharge of the eyes
div.p: From Dioscorides, for a discharge of the eyes. There is a plant called erineos, which grows beside rivers and has leaves like basil. Take one and a half sixths of an ounce of its fruit, and with three ounces of honey anoint the eyes; it will cure the discharge. Its juice, dripped in with sulfur and niter, stops pain of the eye.

div.head: The collyrium called "Light" or "Ray"
div.p: A collyrium called "Light" or "Ray", a one-day repellent remedy, effective against staphylomata, leukomata, scars, trachomas, and old

div.head: [continuing] conditions, and a dry collyrium for trachomas
div.p: [continuing] conditions. Burnt copper, six ounces; roasted washed cadmia, spikenard, hematite stone, Indian lycium, and saffron, four and a half sixths of an ounce of each; white pepper, thirty-three grains; tawny acacia, four and a half ounces; gum, four and a half ounces; enough wine.

A dry collyrium for trachomas and pterygia. Take copper and heat it strongly until glowing, then quench it in the urine of an undefiled child. When the copper, dissolving in the urine, becomes glue-like, set it out to dry in the sun. Then sift it through a fine sieve and take three parts of it, one part of fine black pepper, and add a little Cappadocian salt; anoint once a day.

div.head: Tiberius, adhesive plaster for bone splints and hard swellings
div.p: Tiberius, an adhesive plaster effective against splint-bone growths and hard swellings. If you wish to treat splint-growths forming on the bones without cautery, treat them thus: frankincense, one ounce; ammoniac, one ounce; myrrh and fine flour, one ounce each; copper, one ounce: pound these together, add enough good vinegar, spread on a thick linen cloth, apply it, and bind for seven days.

After this, undo the bandage, foment with warm water, remove the cloth, and let the area breathe; the next day resume the same treatment. It does not work without blood — that is, without first drawing blood.

div.head: Africanus, on the horse with cardiac distress
div.p: By Africanus. "A horse gripped by cardiac distress: first its heart [gives out] ... it stands still, hangs its head low, sweats heavily, and refuses to eat anything offered to it, nor likewise to drink. For such a one there is not much hope of survival." Give it, then, the drenches described above, and administer the rest of the treatment.

div.head: Eumelus's prognosis
div.p: Eumelus's prognosis. A horse's prognosis: if the steps of the hind legs do not reach as far as those of the forelegs, but fall short by about a hand's breadth, and it drags its hooves, and while trotting or leaping the legs lag behind — if then a horse shows these signs, etc.

div.head: For colic from indigestion
div.p: For colic from indigestion. Take sweet flag, pepper, niter, anise, and opopanax in equal parts, and give with old wine. For the remedy's powers must be not only digestive but also warming, so that they may forcibly drive off the undigested food and cause it to be dispersed and the mass arising from it expelled.
And if the animal has pain in the belly, grind pig's knucklebones with wine and administer as a drench.

div.head: Tiberius, on oxen with kidney pain
div.p: Tiberius. If an ox is in pain in the kidneys, the sign is this: blood comes out through the urine, and more fluidly also through the mouth, and likewise through the excrement. The chief sign is that blood flows from the eyes, and the animal walks with legs splayed apart, yet still takes all its food. So great is the effect this affliction has.

Take opopanax, one sixth of an ounce; pepper, one sixth; soak the opopanax in old wine, and likewise boil bay-berries in wine; grind the rest and sift them, mix them into the decoction of bay-berries together with the opopanax, and administer as a drench, anointing the mouth and the anus. It is good, if possible, to anoint the whole ox as well.

div.head: Tiberius, a further remedy for the same
div.p: Tiberius. Crush two heads of garlic carefully in a mortar, add about a half-pint of cold water, mix in the juice of dill, and administer as a drench through the mouth. But if [the text breaks off]

div.head: For overpowering colic, and a plaster for a swollen fetlock
div.p: "[...] if the colic becomes overpowering", etc. Tiberius, an adhesive plaster for a swollen fetlock or for the foot, if it is bruised for any reason and gathers fluid. Fine flour, two ounces; frankincense, one ounce; Colophonian resin, two ounces; ammoniac, one ounce; myrrh, one ounce; dry pitch, two ounces: pound all these and knead with vinegar and a linen cloth; apply it over the swollen part, and over that a sponge full of vinegar-water; renew it for two days, until the medicine sticks fast.
On the third day remove the outer wrappings, leaving the medicine stuck in place.

div.head: Tiberius, for irritation of the sinews
div.p: Tiberius, for irritation of the sinews. Mix equal parts of wheat flour and slaked lime with honey and apply as a poultice; on the third day undo it and foment with the juice of linseed and fenugreek, until it thins out, having first bled the horse; it will be restored to health.
Or boil oil, wine, and common salt together until the salt dissolves, and use.

div.head: On a cut tongue
div.p: On a cut tongue. If the tongue is cut by a rope or by iron, or from a wound or injury, rinse it with old astringent wine; or grind liver-coloured aloe, myrrh, frankincense, and mastic, anoint the wound with comfrey juice, and sprinkle these on. It scars over quickly.

div.head: Tiberius, for meliceris (a cyst)
div.p: Tiberius, for meliceris. Mustard, four ounces; burnt copper, six ounces; Judean bitumen, one ounce; split alum, two ounces; unfired sulfur, two ounces; Alexandrian niter, three ounces; misy, six ounces; enough oleander leaves.

div.head: Tiberius, for karides (warty growths)
div.p: Tiberius, for karides. You shall treat those with karides in troublesome places as Hierocles advises.

div.head: Apsyrtus, on nerve-conditions and wounds affecting the sinews
div.p: Apsyrtus, on nerve-conditions and on wounds affecting the sinews. It happens that a horse with a nerve-condition suffers pain in the neck, etc.; such an animal cannot live. Yet what has been devised by us for wounds of this kind is better: old olive-lees, etc.: remove it promptly and use.

div.head: Tiberius, poultice for thickening of the sinews
div.p: Tiberius, a poultice for thickening of the sinews. Take boiled cypress shoots, a portion of fine flour, and frankincense with old wine, and bind on as a poultice.

div.head: A plaster made with ham fat, for ankyloses
div.p: A plaster made with ham fat, effective against ankyloses and contractures of every joint and tendon, and wherever some thickening has arisen or is restored to normal after a strain. Litharge, three ounces; ham broth, three ounces; galbanum, three ounces; ammoniac incense, one ounce; root of wild cucumber, one ounce: soak the roots of the cucumber for three days, add seawater, and boil together with the wild-olive oil rendered from the ham, until the seawater is absorbed.
Then strain, discard the roots, and let it cool. Then work in the litharge and boil until it no longer stains.

Keep back, from the measure of the broth, six ounces of it, so that when the litharge, having been worked into the sides of the pot, is nearly at the point of not staining, you may then add back the six ounces, and continue boiling together. Then add the ammoniac, and at the end add the galbanum, and turn it out into a mortar.

div.head: A white salve for prolapses
div.p: A white salve for prolapses. Wax, six ounces; bull's suet, six ounces; and niter, likewise.

div.head: A thickening salve
div.p: A thickening salve. Colophonian resin, two ounces; pitch, one ounce; turpentine resin, one ounce; niter, six ounces; wax, one ounce: use with vinegar.

div.head: A softening pre-anointing preparation
div.p: A softening pre-anointing preparation. Fresh goat fat, two ounces; galbanum, two ounces; opopanax, four drachms; cyprus oil, four drachms. This ointment, when applied, neither burns the skin nor causes hair loss.

div.head: How to recognize a horse suffering from colic
div.p: How to recognize a horse suffering from colic. These are the signs of colic: the horse rolls a great deal, does not want to get up, and drinks greedily. Rouse it, then, throw a blanket over it, put a rider on it, and have it driven until it sweats thoroughly. Then bring it into its stall, rub it down carefully, and let it urinate.

div.head: An alternative treatment for colic
div.p: Or pound cumin, roast it with warm oil, and instill it, then give the animal walking exercise; it will then urinate. And after it has urinated, soak fodder in water and give it to chew, and let it rest a while. Then resume the regular feeding. [The text breaks off.]

div.head: To prevent an animal from bruising its sole
div.p: To prevent an animal from bruising its foot. Heat a potsherd until glowing red, add equal parts of wax, lard, and pitch, and make the animal walk on it. Let the potsherd be hollow where the animal sets its foot; do this often — it hardens the feet.

div.head: For when a dam will not accept her newborn
div.p: For when an animal that has given birth does not take to what it has borne. Anoint its teats with brine; for once suckled, the young grows sweet to it and it accepts what it has borne.

div.head: A purgative
div.p: A purgative. Burn vine cuttings and make a distillate from them; administer as a drench for three days. This works equally well on humans.

div.head: Hierocles, on madness and rabies
div.p: Hierocles, on madness and rabies. It happens, as also with men, that the afflicted animal runs about, has bloodshot eyes, and dashes itself against the wall and the manger. Such an animal must be bled at first from the throat, and let much blood flow, and it must be kept from all food.

On the next day, give it panax ground with vinegar to drink, one ounce, for four days, and offer it leeks, and bleed it again from the collarbone. Once it is purged, give it food and care for it as needed. Some, however, say otherwise.

div.head: Apsyrtus, tested drench-recipes for pack animals
div.p: Apsyrtus, tested preparations of drenches for pack animals. Hyssop juice, two draughts; spikenard, storax, dill, and celery, enough of each; leek, one bundle; water, one sextarius: put these into a new pot and boil down to a third, then administer as a drench in this way.

div.head: Another tested remedy, for glanders and chilling
div.p: Another, tested, for glanders and for chill. Make a smooth mixture of goat's milk and white sesame, one measure, warm it lightly, and use.

div.head: Tiberius, drench for the season of green fodder
div.p: Tiberius, a drench for the season of green fodder. Saffron, four drachms; tragacanth, four ounces; Illyrian iris, one ounce; ammoniac, one ounce; sweet wine, four sextarii; oil, one sextarius; eggs, twenty.

div.head: The same author, a drench for autumn
div.p: By the same author, a drench for autumn. Macedonian parsley, one ounce; pepper, four drachms; malabathrum leaf, one ounce; dates, sixty, boiled and ground fine; hydromel, one sextarius; oil, two sextarii; good wine, enough.

div.head: The same author, a drench for summer
div.p: By the same author, a summer drench. Wax, two drachms; costus, one drachm; Illyrian iris, one drachm; cardamom, one drachm; tragacanth, two drachms; honey, one and a half drachms; oil, two sextarii; eggs, twenty; old wine, ten sextarii.

div.head: Pelagonius, for horses discharging fluid from the nostrils
div.p: Pelagonius, for those discharging fluid from the nostrils. The moisture of the nostrils is of various kinds, etc. These must be watched carefully and treated thus: butter or oil with garum.

div.head: Pastille preparation for a drench
div.p: Preparation of pastilles for a drench. Take Alexandrian gum, soak it in old wine, black cassia, six ounces; costus, three ounces; saffron cake, three ounces; white cassia, six ounces; troglitis myrrh, three ounces; aloe, two ounces; sagapenum, five ounces.

div.head: The "charioteers' powder"
div.p: The "charioteers' powder". Reddish cassia, six ounces; black cassia, six ounces; costus, three ounces; galingale, three ounces; wolf's spikenard, six ounces; Sicilian saffron, ten ounces; saffron cake, three ounces; niter, ten ounces.

div.head: A caustic
div.p: A caustic. Ammoniac, six ounces; pine-resin and bitumen, three ounces each; unrefined resin, three ounces; lard, two ounces; wine, three cups.

div.head: Adhesive plaster for lameness
div.p: An adhesive plaster for lameness. Glue, six ounces; pine-resin, six ounces; resin likewise; fine flour, one sextarius; boil sharp vinegar in a cauldron, rub the plaster on the affected hair, and when it comes off, apply it again, until the animal recovers fully.

div.head: A pre-drench against fever
div.p: A pre-drench against fever. Wormwood, southernwood, hyssop, centaury, calamint, and wild vine-shoot, one ounce of each: boil in a pot with water; the next day pour about a sextarius' measure into a horn and drench it through the mouth.

div.head: For greater fevers, given through the mouth
div.p: For greater fevers, given through the mouth. Costus, three ounces; gentian, likewise; opopanax, likewise; panax root, likewise; iris, likewise.

div.head: A fiery salve, and its variant
div.p: A fiery salve. Wax, one ounce; ammoniac, one ounce; resin, six ounces; whole frankincense, six ounces; litharge, three ounces; split alum, six ounces; unripe-olive oil, six ounces.
Another: wax, two ounces; pine-resin, one ounce; bdellium, six ounces; myrrh, three ounces; galbanum, six ounces; opopanax, aloe, and saffron cake, three ounces each; unripe-olive oil.

div.head: Another salve, and a fig salve for animal fat conditions
div.p: Another. Lion fat, six ounces; the suet of a female bull, likewise; wax, six ounces; turpentine resin, the same; sulfur, three ounces; niter, likewise; bay berries, one measure; cassia, six ounces; saffron cake, three ounces; propolis, six ounces; aloe, three ounces.

div.head: On the hoof
div.p: On the hoof. If the hoof develops cracks from above, from the coronet, apply a poultice of ground vetch with vinegar all around, with a sponge over it. Hot fomentation helps; it is better, if you can get it, to use water from a bathhouse's entrance-pool, for it draws something out; if not, use what is to hand.

If there is inflammation, anoint the inflamed part with Cimolian earth and vinegar, together with dung and fine salt; use these warm. If the inflammation persists, boil the Cimolian earth in wine and use it as described above.

div.head: For mange
div.p: For mange. Sharp vinegar, one sextarius; pitch-oil, likewise; niter, one measure: wash and anoint; or lees-oil, one sextarius; unfired sulfur, one ounce; olive lees, one sextarius.

div.head: A wound remedy
div.p: A wound remedy. Tyrrhenian wax, three ounces; verdigris, two ounces; aloe, two ounces; enough old lard: boil and use. It works well for the neck.

div.head: A salve made from figs
div.p: A salve made from figs. Figs, three ounces; niter, six ounces; cypress, one ounce; bull's suet, one measure; manna, one measure; galbanum, one ounce.

div.head: Preparation of pastilles
div.p: Preparation of pastilles. Saffron, three ounces; myrrh, three ounces; cinnamon, one ounce; cassia, two ounces; cardamom, two ounces; sulfur, four ounces; Syrian nard, three ounces; costus, three ounces; Illyrian iris, three ounces, pontic root, three ounces; male frankincense, two ounces; long pepper, three ounces; white pepper, three ounces; mastic flower, three ounces; meum, four ounces; sweet flag, two ounces; saffron cake, four ounces; parsley, three ounces; opopanax, four ounces; iris of Astragalus, four ounces; galingale, three ounces; reed, five ounces; gentian, six ounces; wild carrot, four ounces; storax, four ounces; walnut, four ounces; ginger, three ounces; pure nard, four ounces.

div.head: A short series of preparations: drench, ointment, purgatives, poultice, wound remedy
div.p: A drench. Green celery, one ounce; hyssop, six ounces; pure nard, four ounces; figs, two ounces.
An ointment. Wax, one ounce; pork fat, two ounces; cyprus oil, one ounce.
A purgative. Myrrh, two ounces; opopanax, two ounces; verdigris, two ounces; honey, likewise.
A compound astringent remedy for sores. Frankincense, myrrh, and alum, two ounces of each.
A poultice. Pitch, bitumen, and manna, equal parts; old wine, one sextarius.
A compound purgative. Myrrh, ten ounces; male frankincense, one ounce; opobalsam, one ounce; verdigris, three ounces; honey, four ounces; rose oil, one measure.
A destructive purgative compound. Cinnamon, Syrian nard, mastic flower, and colophony: make into pellets the size of a bean and give in wine, mixing in two ounces of honey.

A wound remedy. Burnt copper, three ounces; copper scale, three ounces; gall-nut, three ounces; pomegranate rind, likewise; split alum and myrrh, two ounces of each; round alum, misy, chalcanthum, hyssop, aphronitron, and frankincense, three ounces of each: dissolve the dry ingredients in vinegar and grind. Then, pouring off the impurities from these, add vinegar and grind separately; afterward mix them together and boil.

div.head: Apollonius's salve, for relaxed sinews and for gout in humans
div.p: Apollonius's salve, effective for relaxed sinews, and also for gout in humans. [Ingredients missing in the damaged text], one ounce; pumice-stone, one ounce: put into a mortar and grind with a lead pestle, until two ounces of lead have been worn away into the mixture, and once it is smooth, set it aside; then put it back into the mortar and grind again with the lead, pouring in three ounces of honey and enough vinegar.

Then pound one ounce of crushed marble, sift it, add cress seed, roast it in a potsherd, grind and sift it; then pound galbanum, take it from the mortar, add deer marrow and enough oil, work all of this in and knead it together, and use it as a salve.

div.head: A salve for relaxed sinews
div.p: A salve for relaxed sinews. Red ochre, one ounce; manna, one ounce; bitumen, one ounce; fine wheat flour, one sextarius; enough old wine: put into a pot together with the rest, ground fine, and boil all together.

div.head: Another, tested remedy
div.p: Another, tested. Wax, one ounce; resin, one ounce; pitch, six ounces; alum, the same amount.

div.head: A remedy for a painful ankle-joint
div.p: A remedy for a painful ankle-joint. Saffron, two ounces; galbanum, two ounces; roasted resin, six ounces; bitumen, six ounces; ammoniac, one ounce; storax oil, one ounce: mix with water and use.

div.head: An arterial remedy
div.p: An arterial remedy. Tragacanth, three minas; saffron, one mina; pepper, eight grams; honey, three minas: dissolve the tragacanth in sweet wine, grind the rest fine, mix together, and use.

div.head: An aromatic troche
div.p: An aromatic troche. Myrrh, ten ounces; cinnamon, three ounces; frankincense, three ounces; cassia, eight drachms; pepper, three drachms; bdellium, five drachms; reed, five drachms; celery seed and Illyrian iris, two drachms of each: dissolve in old wine and use.

div.head: A restorative for weak animals, and a universal salve
div.p: A restorative for weak or failing animals. Bdellium, galbanum, manna, ammoniac, resin, and Illyrian iris, equal parts of each; wax, double that amount: take up in cyprus oil.

A universal salve. Pepper, one ounce; galbanum, one ounce; myrrh, one ounce; Cretan aristolochia, one ounce; Illyrian iris, one ounce; peucedanum, three ounces; saffron, one ounce; mulberry sap, one ounce; pyrethrum, one ounce; Cnidian grain, four ounces; cardamom, one ounce; opobalsam, two ounces; cardamom seed, one ounce; iris oil, a sixth of an ounce; enough wax.

div.head: Fabricianus's troches for glanders and foot-bruises
div.p: Fabricianus's troches, for glanders and for foot-bruises. Cinnamon, three ounces; cassia, three ounces; myrrh, likewise; sagapenum, five ounces; saffron, two ounces; frankincense, four ounces; niter, one ounce: grind these well with water, shape into well-sized troches, and use with hydromel.

div.head: For distress in draught animals, and two further remedies for the nostrils
div.p: For distress in draught animals. Cut the bark of the dog-rose and give it to eat while fasting, or give about two cotylae of its broth to drink, and grind manna and give with wine, and bathe copiously with warm water.
Another. Dissolve sandarach in water and pour it into the nostrils.
Another. Grind hellebore, dissolve it in water, and pour it into the nostrils; and if you also mix it, crushed, into chaff, it has the same effect. Let it be given in a fairly large quantity.

div.head: Composition of the "gleukirinon" preparation
div.p: Composition of the gleukirinon. Iris oil, three ounces; unfermented must, fifteen ounces; reed, one ounce; spikenard, four bundles; galingale, two ounces; aromatic cypress, two ounces; costus, six ounces, and troglitis myrrh, two ounces; cassia, one ounce; last year's bay leaves, two ounces; amomum, four ounces. Pound all these fine, put them with the oil and the must into a new pot, and boil.

div.head: Apsyrtus's aromatic and bitter drenches
div.p: Apsyrtus's preparation of an aromatic drench. Malabathrum leaf, half an ounce; costus, three ounces; spikenard-ear, half an ounce; melilot, one ounce; Cretan nard, half an ounce; amomum, half an ounce; balsam-fruit, half an ounce; Illyrian iris, one ounce; mastic flower, one ounce; marjoram, one ounce; cassia, one ounce.
By the same author, another preparation of a bitter drench. Peucedanum, gentian, and colocynth, three ounces of each; centaury, four ounces; aloe, two ounces; wormwood, three ounces.

div.head: Further drenches, and a remedy for pneumonia
div.p: A thickening drench. Troglitis myrrh, four ounces; aloe and cassia, two ounces of each; iris, one ounce; comfrey, five ounces; calamint, three ounces; with wine and boiled must.
For pneumonia. Steep saffron cake strongly in dark wine together with large fleshy dates and pine nuts, grind smooth with honey, and administer as a drench in wine.
A relaxing drench. Cumin, parsley, celery, and coriander, one ounce of each; cabbage, two ounces; cardamom, likewise.
Another, "for every pain". Wine and costus, one ounce of each; fennel and white pepper and myrrh, one ounce of each.

div.head: A final compound purgative, and a proverb
div.p: A compound purgative. Myrrh, ten ounces; male frankincense and rose oil, one ounce of each; verdigris, one ounce; honey, four ounces.
When God gives, envy has no power; and when he gives not, toil has no power.
